# Exact polygon replacement for finitely many planar cap volumes

## 1. Statement

Let K be a planar convex body and let H_1,...,H_m be finitely many closed
halfplanes. There is a planar convex polygon Q satisfying

    |Q|=|K|,       |Q intersect H_i|=|K intersect H_i| for all i.  (1)

More strongly, Q can preserve the area in every open cell of the finite
line arrangement determined by their boundaries. Such polygons can be
chosen arbitrarily close to K in Hausdorff distance.

The replacement need not be contained in K or contain K. Requiring both
containment in K and equal total area would prohibit replacement of a
nonpolygonal body. This theorem imposes no such requirement.

This is an ordinary planar statement (n=0). Its proof does not provide
general higher-dimensional or mixed-fiber replacement automatically.

## 2. Exact correction in exposed boundary cells

We first record a lemma valid in any finite ambient dimension. Let a finite
hyperplane arrangement partition space into open full-dimensional cells R.
Suppose an outer polytope approximation P contains K and is already exact
in every cell except a finite list of cells R_i. Suppose each R_i contains
an exposed point p_i of K. For sufficiently close outer approximations,
the remaining cell-volume errors can be corrected independently by finitely
many planar truncations.

Indeed choose a unit exposing normal n_i, with unique support point p_i,
and let b_i=h_K(n_i). The compact caps
K intersect {n_i dot x>=b_i-delta} shrink to p_i as delta decreases to zero:
any limit point belongs to the unique supporting face. Therefore choose
delta_i>0 so that this entire compact cap lies inside the open cell R_i.
It has positive full-dimensional volume, because its threshold is below
the support value of a body with interior.

For all sufficiently close outer polytopes P, the corresponding cap
P intersect {n_i dot x>=b_i-delta_i} also lies in R_i. Otherwise bounded
counterexample points would converge to a point of the compact K-cap
outside R_i, a contradiction. Its volume is bounded below by the positive
K-cap volume. Meanwhile the cell-volume excess

    Delta_i=|P intersect R_i|-|K intersect R_i|

is nonnegative and tends to zero, being at most |P|-|K|. The function

    t -> |P intersect {n_i dot x>t}|

is continuous, because hyperplanes have zero ambient volume. Between
t=b_i-delta_i and t=max_P n_i dot x it ranges from a value greater than
Delta_i to zero. Choose t_i giving exactly Delta_i and truncate by
n_i dot x<=t_i.

Each removed cap lies wholly in its own arrangement cell. Consequently
the corrections do not affect any other cell and commute with one another.
The final polytope has exactly the target cell volumes. The cuts lie near
K; by first taking each delta_i arbitrarily small and then taking P close,
the final polytope can be kept arbitrarily Hausdorff close to K.

## 3. Elementary density of exposed points among planar extreme points

Every extreme point p of a planar convex body is a limit of exposed points.
Here is the needed planar proof. If p is exposed there is nothing to prove.
Otherwise choose a supporting line at p. Its face is a segment and p must
be one endpoint, because p is extreme. Let n be its outward normal, and
let v be tangent to the line, pointing toward p along this segment.

For t>0 maximize (n+t v) dot x on K. Any sequence of maximizers as t tends
to zero has its limit in the original supporting face. Comparing with p
also gives v dot x>=v dot p for every maximizer, so the only possible limit
is p. The convex scalar support function

    h(t)=max_(x in K) (n+t v) dot x

is differentiable except at countably many t: its left and right derivative
intervals at distinct nondifferentiability points are disjoint, and each
nonempty interval contains a rational number. At a differentiability point
all maximizers have the same v-coordinate h'(t), and their n-coordinate
is then h(t)-t h'(t). Since n,v are independent, the maximizer is unique.
Choosing differentiability points tending to zero proves the assertion.

## 4. Cells without exposed points are polygonal

Let R be an open arrangement cell with positive area intersection with K,
and suppose R contains no exposed boundary point of K. Put

    L=K intersect closure(R).

Every extreme point of L lies on a cell wall. In fact an extreme point of
L in the open cell would be extreme in K: if it lay in a nontrivial K-segment,
a small subsegment would remain inside R. The density statement just proved
would then give exposed K-points in the open cell, contradicting the
hypothesis.

There are finitely many cell walls. On any one wall, an extreme point of L
must be an endpoint of the compact interval L intersect that wall, so only
finitely many such points are possible. Hence L is a polygon. To see this
last conclusion without an additional representation theorem, any point
of a planar convex body lies on a chord with boundary endpoints; each
boundary endpoint belongs to a supporting segment whose endpoints are
extreme. Thus the body is the convex hull of its extreme points.

Each facet inequality of L is either a cell-wall inequality or the inequality
of a supporting line of K. For a facet not contained in a cell wall, choose
a relative interior point of that facet lying inside R. Its boundary and
supporting side locally agree with K, so its line supports all of K by
convexity. Add all these finitely many genuine K-supporting lines to the
outer polytope approximation. Then inside R its intersection is already
exactly L intersect R: the other inequalities describing L are supplied
by the cell walls themselves. Thus these cells acquire zero area excess.

## 5. Empty cells, full cells, and the construction

Use every open full-dimensional arrangement cell. If K misses a cell R,
separate the compact convex set K from the open convex set R. There is a
closed halfplane containing K whose intersection with R is empty: weak
separation is strict on the R side because R is open and the separating
normal is nonzero. Add this halfplane to the outer approximation. This
also covers cells whose closures merely touch K.

If R contains no boundary point of K but meets K, connectedness implies
R is contained in the interior of K. It is already exact in any outer
approximation. Such a cell is necessarily bounded, since K is bounded.

For every remaining cell with no exposed K-boundary point, use Section 4
to add its finitely many genuine supporting lines. All these added
halfplanes contain K. Intersect them with arbitrarily close circumscribed
polygons of K; the result is still an arbitrarily close outer polygon.
Existence of the latter follows, for example, from finite increasingly
dense sets of support-normal directions: their intersections are uniformly
bounded and their limit satisfies every support inequality of K.

Every cell not yet exact now contains an exposed K-boundary point. Apply
Section 2 to correct its nonnegative excess, independently in each such
cell. This yields exact equality of every cell area. The arrangement lines
themselves have area zero. Every original closed halfplane is a union of
some open cells and parts of those lines, so all identities (1) follow.

## 6. Exact scope for extremal reductions

If a fixed finite cap family covers the entire ambient plane and its
volumes at K certify an attained minimum value, preserving those volumes
and the total area gives the same upper bound at the replacement polygon.
The global extremal definition supplies the reverse bound. This is a valid
replacement at that finite cap certificate; it does not assert that an
arbitrary chosen cap family covers a changed body.

In higher dimensions, the no-exposed-cell step is the missing part of this
proof. A cell wall can meet K in a curved lower-dimensional body, so finitely
many walls no longer give finitely many extreme points of their intersections.
A middle band of a cylinder is the basic example. Independent cap trims
also cannot be presumed to correct such coupled boundary pieces.
